answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. It appears in The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, chapter 3, in the section headed “Of Prayer, of Love, and of Contact with other Worlds” — spoken by the dying elder Zosima. The familiar English wording is Constance Garnett’s translation, and it is confirmed word for word in the Project Gutenberg text ↗ and in a scanned Heinemann printing.

source.excerpt: Brothers, have no fear of men’s sin. Love a man even in his sin, for that is the semblance of Divine Love and is the highest love on earth. Love all God’s creation, the whole and every grain of sand in it. Love every leaf, every ray of God’s light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you will perceive the divine mystery in things.
trail: The full Garnett text at Project Gutenberg ↗ contains the sentence verbatim in Book VI, chapter 3; the same record credits Constance Garnett as translator and marks the text public domain in the USA.
The English Wikisource chapter ↗ places it under the subsection heading “(g) Of Prayer, of Love, and of Contact with other Worlds.”
A scanned Heinemann printing ↗, catalogued as London, 1912, carries the same wording on the page image — independent of the modern digital transcriptions.
Wikiquote ↗ lists it among the sourced quotations, under The Brothers Karamazov (1879–1880), Book VI, Chapter 3, Garnett translation.

source.rightsNote: Both layers are clear. The Russian original was serialized in The Russian Messenger from January 1879 to November 1880, and the English wording quoted here is Constance Garnett’s translation, published in 1912 — comfortably before the 1931 US cutoff. Project Gutenberg ↗ states the Garnett text is public domain in the USA. Note that this applies to Garnett specifically; later twentieth- and twenty-first-century translations of the same sentence are separate works and may still be in copyright.

author.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Fyodor Dostoevsky (born 11 November 1821, died 9 February 1881) wrote Crime and Punishment, Notes from Underground, Demons and The Brothers Karamazov, novels that made moral argument into plot. He served four years at hard labour in Siberia for belonging to a banned discussion circle, an experience that turned a young radical into a writer obsessed with guilt, faith and forgiveness. The Brothers Karamazov ran as a serial from January 1879 to November 1880; he died the following February.

misattribution.heading: Two things the meme version drops
misattribution.intro: The credit to Dostoevsky is correct — this is not one of the fabricated lines that collect around his name. But the version that circulates as a standalone aphorism quietly loses two facts, and both change what you are reading.

items.why: The words belong to the dying elder Zosima, inside a chapter Garnett titles “Conversations and Exhortations of Father Zossima ↗.” Dostoevsky wrote them, but he wrote them as a monk answering an atheist — not as a personal maxim signed in his own name.

“Semblance of Divine Love” is Garnett’s 1912 rendering. Dostoevsky’s Russian reads “подобие божеской любви ↗” — a likeness of divine love. Other translators phrase it differently, which is why a search for these exact words finds Garnett’s text and not the others.

misattribution.truthLine: So: genuinely Dostoevsky, genuinely in the novel, genuinely at this page — but it is Zosima speaking, in Garnett’s English. The full sentence, which the short version cuts, is “Love a man even in his sin, for that is the semblance of Divine Love and is the highest love on earth,” as printed in the Project Gutenberg text ↗.

context.heading: Why Dostoevsky put it in a monk’s mouth
lead: The sentence sits in Book VI, “The Russian Monk,” which follows immediately on Book V, “Pro and Contra” — the two chapters in which Ivan Karamazov lays out the case against God: chapter IV, “Rebellion,” and chapter V, “The Grand Inquisitor.” Having given the prosecution its strongest possible speech, Dostoevsky answers it not with an argument but with an old man’s deathbed talk.

Zosima’s reply is deliberately unimpressive as logic. It does not refute Ivan; it changes the subject to practice. “Love a man even in his sin” is the hinge — the claim that loving people at their worst is not tolerance or excuse-making but the nearest a human being gets to how God is said to love, and therefore the highest form the thing takes on earth.
context.detailsSummary: What comes next in the passage
detailsBody: The line is the opening of a cascade. Zosima moves straight from sinners to creation at large: love every leaf, every ray of light, the animals, the plants, the grain of sand. The logic is that love is one faculty, not several — you cannot practise it selectively and expect it to work.

He then singles out children as “sinless like the angels,” and credits a fellow wanderer, Father Anfim, with teaching him to love them — a small, concrete memory dropped into the middle of a sermon, which is characteristic of how Dostoevsky keeps Zosima from sounding like a tract.
context.pull: Dostoevsky gives the atheist the better speech, then answers him with a dying monk who never argues back.

Wikiquote lists 'Love a man even in his sin, for that is the semblance of Divine Love and is the highest love on earth.' as a sourced quotation from The Brothers Karamazov (1879-1880), Book VI, Chapter 3, Constance Garnett translation.

An Internet Archive scan catalogued as The Brothers Karamazov, trans. Constance Garnett, William Heinemann Ltd, London, 1912, contains the sentence 'Brothers, have no fear of men's sin. Love a man even in his sin, for that is the semblance of Divine Love and is the highest love on earth.'

The Russian original chapter reads 'Братья, не бойтесь греха людей, любите человека и во грехе его, ибо сие уж подобие божеской любви и есть верх любви на земле.' in Книга шестая, III, section 'ж) О молитве, о любви и о соприкосновении мирам иным'.
The Brothers Karamazov was published as a serial in The Russian Messenger from January 1879 to November 1880, and Constance Garnett published a translation in 1912.
Fyodor Dostoevsky was born 11 November 1821 and died 9 February 1881; he was a Russian novelist, short-story writer, essayist and journalist.
